transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I... I came in because I know the people at my apartment are watching my comings and goings. They're slipping notes about me to the office. Everybody keeps telling me it's just regular notices on the doors, like for water shut-offs or whatever, but I know better. It's like that time back in '98 when I was working at the hardware store—well, not working exactly, just helping out my buddy Earl. Earl had this dog, a beagle mix, that would just stare at you. Never barked, just stared. Anyway, these notes at my apartment, they're not just notices. They're watching me.
Do you think these people are watching you for a specific reason?

Well, I... I don't know exactly why. I just know they are. Like I was saying, they're tracking when I leave and come back, slipping those notes to the office. People keep telling me, "Oh, it's just a notice about the parking lot," or the water, but I know it's about me. They just want to know my business. 

It's like... well, it's like the guy who runs the office. He wears these real thick glasses. Actually, they look exactly like the glasses my Uncle Pete used to wear. Uncle Pete drove a truck for, oh, gotta be thirty years. Hauling lumber, mostly. He used to take me in the cab with him sometimes when I was a kid, back before they had all those strict rules about passengers. We’d stop at this little diner off the highway and get cherry pie. They just don't make pie like that anymore. The crust was always real flaky, you know? Used to get it with a big scoop of vanilla ice cream right on top...
Do you feel like your thoughts are connected and make sense when you're talking about these things?

Well, I... I guess so, most of the time. But lately, when I try to explain things, it's like... I start talking about paying the rent, right? And then I'm talking about the marina down by the lake. I used to go down there and watch the boats. My cousin had a little aluminum fishing boat with a 10-horsepower Evinrude motor on it. We'd take it out early, before the sun even came up. It was so quiet out there on the water. 

Anyway, I'll be talking about the rent, then the marina, and then suddenly I'm talking about the choir robes from church, and the wires they put in the walls... and people just look at me. They look at me like I skipped half the story, you know? Like they have no idea how I got from point A to point B. But it all makes sense in my head while I'm saying it. It's just... it's like trying to untangle a fishing line. You pull one end and the whole thing just knots up worse.
Do you often find it difficult to stay on one topic when talking to others?

Well, yeah, I suppose I do. Like I was saying just a minute ago, I'll start off trying to explain something simple, right? Like... like paying the rent. And then, before I know it, I'm talking about the marina, and then the choir robes, and those wires they put in the walls. 

It's funny I brought up the choir robes, actually. We used to wear these deep burgundy ones back at the First Baptist. They had these gold sashes. My mother made sure mine was always pressed crisp. She had this old iron, one of those heavy ones you had to be careful with or you'd scorch the fabric. She was always so particular about ironing. She'd set up the board right in the middle of the kitchen on Sunday mornings while the roast was in the oven. You could smell the beef cooking while she pressed the robes... 

But yeah, I'll be talking about all that, the rent and the wires, and people just stare at me. They look at me like I completely skipped half the story. Like they don't see how one thing leads to the next.
Do you feel like your thoughts are jumping from one thing to another without any connection when this happens?

Well, like I just said, to me it doesn't feel like they're jumping. There's a string there, you know? But to everyone else... yeah, I guess they don't see the connection. Because I'll be trying to explain something plain as day, like paying the rent, and then suddenly I'm onto the marina, and the choir robes, and the wires in the walls. And they just stare at me like I skipped half the story. 

Speaking of those wires, though, I'm pretty sure they used copper in my building. You know how expensive copper got a few years back? People were stealing it right out of the air conditioning units behind the strip mall down the road. Just gutting them in the middle of the night. My buddy Earl used to scrap metal, but he never stole it. He mostly just collected aluminum cans and old radiators he'd find on the curb. He had this beat-up Ford Ranger, the tailgate was rusted clean through, and we'd drive around on trash day looking for anything heavy. He made decent money doing that for a while, before his back gave out.
Do you ever hear voices or sounds that other people can't hear?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I hear the regular sounds, you know? The traffic, the radiator hissing. But no voices or anything like that. 

Although, the radiator in my place has been acting up lately. It makes this loud clanking noise right around 3:00 AM. Clank, clank, clank. It wakes me up every time. I tried telling the super about it, this guy named Hector. He's a nice enough guy, always wears these bright yellow work boots. I asked him where he got them once, and he said his brother sent them all the way from Texas. His brother works on an oil rig down there, I think. That's a tough job, being out on the water like that for weeks at a time. I don't think I could do it. I get seasick just looking at a boat swaying at the dock. 

Anyway, Hector said he'd come look at the radiator, but he hasn't shown up yet. So I just lie there in the dark, listening to it clank. But no, to answer your question, no voices or anything. Just the radiator.
Do you really believe that the people in your apartment building are watching you and slipping notes to the office about your activities?

Well, yeah, I do. Because I know they're watching my comings and goings. They keep an eye on when I leave and when I get back, and they're slipping those notes about me to the front office. Everybody keeps telling me it's just regular notices on the doors, like for water shutoffs or whatever, but I know what's really going on. 

Speaking of those doors, though, they painted them all this awful shade of green last summer. Like a split-pea soup kind of green. The painters they hired left a total mess, too. Left masking tape stuck to the hinges, paint drops all over the carpet in the hallway. I remember when I used to do some painting work with my uncle Pete down in Florida, back when I was a teenager. We used to paint these big motels along the highway. Pete was a real stickler for drop cloths. If you spilled even one drop of primer on the concrete, he'd chew you out for an hour straight. He smoked those unfiltered cigarettes, always had one hanging right out the side of his mouth while he yelled at you. He died of emphysema back in '98... or maybe it was '99. 

But yeah, they think I don't see them slipping those notes to the office, but I definitely do.
Do you think your way of talking and jumping between topics is different from how you used to talk in the past?

Well, yeah, I guess it is different. Like I was saying before, when I try to explain things now, I'll start with something normal, like paying the rent, and then I'm onto the marina, then the choir robes, and the wires in the walls. And people just look at me like I skipped half the story. It didn't use to be like that. 

I used to be pretty good at explaining things, especially back when I worked at the hardware store. I was the guy everyone came to when they needed to figure out what kind of plumbing fittings they needed. Plumbings a tricky thing, you know? You get the wrong threading on a PVC pipe, and the whole sink leaks. We had this one customer, Mrs. Gable, she tried to fix her own garbage disposal and ended up flooding her whole kitchen. I had to go over there after my shift to help her mop it up. She made a real good cherry pie, though. Baked it from scratch with the lattice crust on top. You don't see lattice crusts much anymore. People just buy those frozen Marie Callender pies. Which are alright, I guess, if you're in a hurry. But it's not the same. 

But yeah, the way I talk now... people just stare at me like they're lost.
Do you think your thoughts are as organized as they used to be?

Well, no, they're definitely not as organized. That's the thing. When I try to explain things, like I said, I'll start talking about the rent, and then suddenly I'm talking about the marina, and then the choir robes, and those wires I know they put in the walls. And people just look at me like I skipped half the story. 

It reminds me of when I was trying to organize my tool shed last spring. I had all these coffee cans full of nails and screws. My grandfather used to keep his nails in old Folgers cans. He had this massive workbench out in his garage in Ohio. We used to go visit him every Thanksgiving. We'd drive all the way from here, packed into this old station wagon my dad had. It had that fake wood paneling on the sides, you know? And the vinyl seats that would burn your legs if you parked in the sun. We'd play the license plate game for hours. I think I saw a plate from Hawaii once, which didn't make any sense, being in the middle of the country and all. 

But yeah, my thoughts... they just kind of go all over the place now, and I end up talking about the wires and the marina instead of what I started with.
Do you think your mind is playing tricks on you when you start talking about one thing and then jump to something completely different?

Well, maybe my mind is playing tricks, I don't know. It's just... like I was saying, I'll be trying to explain something simple, like the rent being due, and before I know it, I'm going on about the marina down by the lake, and then the choir robes from church, and those wires they hid in the walls. And the person I'm talking to just stares at me, like I skipped half the story. 

I used to go to that marina a lot, actually. My buddy Tom had a little aluminum fishing boat docked there. We'd take it out early on Saturday mornings, before the sun even came up. We used to catch some huge catfish out near the dam. Tom had this special bait he made himself out of chicken livers and garlic powder. Smelled absolutely terrible, but the fish loved it. He kept it in this old Tupperware container that his wife got mad at him for ruining. She was always mad at him about something, though. I think they ended up getting divorced back in... oh, must have been 2012. She took the house and the dog, but he got to keep the boat. 

But yeah, my mind... I guess it just jumps around, and I end up talking about the wires and the robes when I was supposed to be talking about the rent.
Have you always had a tendency to jump between different topics when talking, or is this something that has developed over time?

No, it wasn't always like this. It's something that kind of... crept up on me over time, I guess. Like I keep telling you, it's just happening nowadays where I try to explain things, and I'll start with the rent, and then I'm on about the marina, and the choir robes, and the wires in the walls. And people just look at me like I skipped half the story. 

I never had that problem back in the day. Back when I was in school... well, I didn't finish high school, you know. Left in the eleventh grade because I got a job at the lumber yard. My Uncle Frank got it for me. He was a big guy, always wore these heavy-duty suspenders that had little tape measures printed all over them. He thought it was the funniest thing. Bought them at a flea market down in Florida when he went to visit his sister. I went to Florida once, but it's way too hot. The humidity just settles right in your chest and you can't breathe. Plus the bugs down there are the size of your fist. Palmetto bugs, they call them, but they're just giant cockroaches if you ask me. I don't know how people live with them, crawling up the walls and all. 

But anyway, yeah, I didn't used to talk like this. It just developed over time, I suppose.
Have you experienced any periods in the past where you had these thoughts of being watched for more than a month?

Yeah, it's been a lot longer than a month. I'd say those suspicious thoughts... you know, about the apartment neighbors and the leasing office... they've been with me for about a year and a month now. 

It started right around the time they were supposed to come fix the boiler down in the basement. The maintenance guy, he was always walking around wearing these heavy work boots that left black scuff marks all over the linoleum in the hallway. I tried getting those marks out once with some baking soda and a wet rag. My mother swore by baking soda for just about everything. She used to keep an open box in the back of the refrigerator to stop the milk from tasting like whatever else was in there. Usually it was onions, because she made this beef stew almost every Sunday. Cooked it in a big cast-iron pot that weighed an absolute ton. You had to rub those pots down with vegetable oil or they'd rust right through. I left one out in the rain once when we were camping up near the state park, and it was completely orange by morning. We were sleeping in this old canvas tent that smelled like mildew, and it rained for three days straight. 

But anyway, yeah, it's been about thirteen months, a year and a month, since I started realizing the neighbors and the office folks were keeping tabs on me.
Do you think there's anything wrong with the way you're putting your thoughts into words when we talk?

Well, I mean... I don't know if there's something *wrong* exactly, but like I've been saying, it just gets all jumbled up. I try to explain things, just regular things, and I'll start with the rent being due, right? But then I'm talking about the marina, and then the choir robes, and those wires they hid in the walls. And people just look at me like I skipped half the story. 

It's frustrating, because I know what I want to say. Like when I try to talk to the guy at the grocery store. The one on Fifth Street, not the big chain one. The big chain ones always move everything around so you can't find the coffee filters. I used to drink three pots of coffee a day back when I worked at the lumber yard. Black, no sugar. Sugar rots your teeth out. My dentist told me that when I was twelve, Dr. Henderson. He had these big thick glasses that magnified his eyes so he looked like an owl leaning over you with that drill. I hated that drill. The sound of it just goes right through your skull. 

But yeah, I guess the way I put my thoughts into words... it just doesn't come out right, and they just stare at me like I'm not making any sense.
Do you have times when your thoughts seem to flow and connect normally, without jumping between topics?

Not really, no. I mean, I wish I did. But like I keep telling you, I just can't seem to string it together normally anymore. Every time I try to explain things, I end up doing exactly what I said before—I'll start out talking about the rent, and then suddenly I'm on about the marina, and the choir robes, and those wires in the walls. I know I keep bringing that up, but it's just the best way I can describe it. 

Speaking of the choir robes, my Aunt Linda used to wear one of those big maroon ones. She sang alto down at the First Methodist. Had a voice like an absolute foghorn, God rest her soul. She used to practice her hymns in the kitchen while she was boiling potatoes. She made the best potato salad, always put a little bit of paprika on top so it looked real fancy in the bowl. We'd eat it out on the back porch on the Fourth of July, watching the fireworks go off over the lake. The mosquitoes were just terrible by that lake, though. You had to light those little green coils that smelled like cheap incense just to sit out there for five minutes without getting eaten alive. I don't know what they put in those coils, probably something toxic if you breathe it in too long. 

But anyway... no, my thoughts just don't connect right. I try to stay on one thing, but they just scatter, and people just give me that look, like I skipped half the story, and I can't ever seem to get back on track.
Do you feel like your way of thinking and talking is causing you problems in your daily life or relationships?

Yeah, it... it really is causing problems. I mean, I've fallen way behind on my bills. The electric, the water... I just can't keep my days organized anymore. And I've missed a bunch of appointments, too. I even stopped showing up for church and the volunteer stuff I used to do down at the food pantry. I just can't trust ordinary interactions with people, you know? It's like I don't know what they're really thinking or what they're going to do.

Speaking of the food pantry, we used to get these huge pallets of canned green beans. Just boxes and boxes of them. People always donated green beans, but nobody ever brought in corn. I always preferred corn, especially the creamed kind. My grandmother used to make creamed corn from scratch, scraping the cobs with this old silver butter knife she got as a wedding present. It had a little rose pattern on the handle that was mostly worn off. She kept all her good silver in a wooden box lined with blue velvet. It smelled like cedar and old perfume in there. She wouldn't let us touch it unless it was Thanksgiving. We had this big turkey one year that wouldn't even fit in the oven, so my uncle had to take it out to the garage and deep fry it in a turkey fryer. He nearly burned the garage down because he put it in while it was still frozen, and the oil just splattered everywhere. It took weeks to get the grease stains off the concrete floor.

But yeah, I just... I can't keep things straight, and I've stopped going to things because I just can't handle being around people or keeping my schedule organized.
Do you think your thoughts are disorganized only when you are talking about the people watching you, or is it like that with most things you try to discuss?

It's... it's with most things, really. Not just the people watching me. I mean, I try to explain things, just regular everyday things, and I'll start out talking about the rent being due, and then somehow I'm talking about the marina, and then the choir robes, and the wires they put in the walls. And people just look at me like I skipped half the story. 

I used to go down to the marina all the time when I was younger. My buddy Dave had this little aluminum fishing boat with a sputtering outboard motor that always smelled like gasoline and lake weed. We'd take it out early, before the sun even came up, trying to catch bass. Dave always brought these terrible sandwiches his wife made—bologna and sweet pickles on white bread that would get all soggy in the cooler. The cooler was this bright orange Coleman one, the kind with the white handle that would pinch your fingers if you weren't careful. I pinched my thumb in it once so bad the nail turned black and fell off three weeks later. It was right before I had to help my brother move a piano into his second-floor apartment. Moving a piano with a missing thumbnail is just about the worst thing you can do. The guy at the hardware store told me to soak it in Epsom salts, but I don't think that actually does anything. Epsom salts always just leave a gritty film on the bottom of the tub that you have to scrub out later with a brush. 

But yeah, it's... it's everything I try to talk about. The words just get all tangled up no matter what the subject is.
Has your way of thinking and talking always been like this, or is this something that has changed over time?

No, it hasn't always been like this. It really started changing... I'd say about a year and five months ago. That's when I left the house I shared with my wife and moved into this senior apartment complex. 

My wife, she always kept the house so spotless. We had this big oak dining table that she'd polish every Sunday afternoon. She used that lemon-scented Pledge, you know? The smell of it would just hang in the air all evening. We bought that table at an estate sale out in the county, from this old farmhouse that had a wraparound porch and a rusted-out tractor in the front yard. The guy selling it was wearing these thick suspenders and kept chewing on a toothpick the whole time we were haggling. He had a dog, too, a golden retriever mix that just laid on the porch thumping its tail against the floorboards. I always wanted a dog, but my wife said they track too much mud into the house. She was right, I suppose. Mud is terrible to get out of those Berber carpets. We had beige Berber in the living room, and if you spilled even a drop of coffee on it, it would just soak right in and spread like a bruise. I tried using that foaming carpet cleaner once, the kind in the aerosol can with the little plastic scrub brush on the cap, but it just made the spot look cleaner than the rest of the carpet, which was almost worse. 

But anyway, yeah, the thinking and the talking getting all messed up... that started when I moved into the senior apartment, about a year and five months back.
Did you used to be able to keep your thoughts organized and on track when talking to people before you moved into the senior apartment?

Yeah, before I moved, I was fine. I could hold a regular conversation. Like I was saying a few minutes ago, about how now I'll start on the rent and end up on the marina and the choir robes and the wires they put in the walls... and how people look at me like I skipped half the story? I never used to do that. It wasn't like that at all. 

Back at the old house, I could just stand out by the chain-link fence and talk to Mr. Henderson for an hour straight, no problem, just keeping right on track. He was our next-door neighbor, the one with the huge vegetable garden. He grew these massive beefsteak tomatoes, big as softballs. He always told me his secret was crushing up dried eggshells and mixing them right into the dirt. We ate a lot of eggs back then so I'd save the shells for him. My wife usually made them scrambled in this heavy cast-iron skillet she got from her mother. You couldn't wash that pan with soap, though. You had to just wipe it out with a paper towel and rub vegetable oil into it while it was still warm. I always thought that was a little unsanitary, just leaving the old grease in there, but she said it seasoned the metal. We kept the oil in this little glass bottle by the stove, but the stopper got glued shut with grease once, and I had to run it under hot water for twenty minutes just to loosen it. The hot water in that house was incredible, though. We had a brand new water heater put in after the basement flooded back in the late nineties, and it would get so hot it could practically take your skin off if you turned the handle too far to the left. 

But yeah, I used to be able to just tell a story from start to finish without losing my place.
Do you have days where your thoughts seem more connected and easier to explain to others than they do right now?

Not really. I mean... even on the days where maybe I can string a few more sentences together and sound a little clearer, it doesn't matter much. Because for most of the time since I moved into that apartment, I just feel so low. Just useless. I don't even have any interest in the things I used to like doing. 

Like the woodworking. I used to love whittling these little wooden birds out of basswood blocks. Basswood is the best for that because the grain is so tight and it doesn't splinter when you make a fine cut. I had this set of carving knives that came in a leather roll-up pouch. The leather smelled like a saddle shop, you know? Like oil and dust. I bought them from a catalogue that used to come in the mail every month. The mail carrier back then was this guy named Phil who always wore shorts, even in December. He said his legs never got cold, which I always thought was a lie. You can't walk through six inches of snow in shorts and not get cold. Snow gets right into the tops of your boots if you don't wear those gaiter things. I bought a pair of gaiters once for a hunting trip, but they had these plastic snaps that broke the very first time I tried to put them on. Plastic just gets brittle in the cold. It's like those cheap ice scrapers they give away at the gas station—you push too hard on the windshield and the handle snaps right off in your glove. 

But yeah, even if my thoughts are a little less tangled some days, I still just sit there feeling empty and useless, not caring about the carving or anything else.
Do you ever see things that aren't really there?

See things? No, I don't... I don't think I've ever seen anything that wasn't there. I mean, my eyesight isn't what it used to be. I had to get bifocals about three years ago because I couldn't read the labels on the soup cans at the grocery store. They make the print so small now, especially on the low-sodium ones. My wife used to buy the low-sodium chicken noodle because she read in a magazine that regular soup has too much salt and it's bad for your blood pressure. The magazine was one of those ones they always have at the dentist's office, with the glossy pages that stick together if somebody spilled coffee on them. Our dentist had this waiting room with these horrible orange vinyl chairs that made a squeaking noise every time you shifted your weight. He had a fish tank in there, too, with these little neon tetras that just swam back and forth all day. I always felt bad for them, stuck in that little glass box with fake plastic plants. Real plants are so much better for aquariums because they help oxygenate the water. I tried to grow a fern once in the living room, but it just turned brown and crispy at the edges. I think it was too close to the heating vent. Those vents would blow hot air right on the curtains and make them billow out like sails on a ship. 

But no, I don't see things that aren't there. Just... just regular things, mostly.

My buddy Earl used to scrap metal, but he never stole it. He mostly just collected aluminum cans and old radiators he'd find on the curb. He had this beat-up Ford Ranger, the tailgate was rusted clean through, and we'd drive around on trash day looking for anything heavy. That's a tough job, being out on the water like that for weeks at a time. I don't think I could do it. I get seasick just looking at a boat swaying at the dock. 

Anyway, Hector said he'd come look at the radiator, but he hasn't shown up yet. So I just lie there in the dark, listening to it clank. But no, to answer your question, no voices or anything. Just the radiator.

He smoked those unfiltered cigarettes, always had one hanging right out the side of his mouth while he yelled at you. He died of emphysema back in '98... or maybe it was '99.

She used to keep an open box in the back of the refrigerator to stop the milk from tasting like whatever else was in there. Usually it was onions, because she made this beef stew almost every Sunday. Cooked it in a big cast-iron pot that weighed an absolute ton. You had to rub those pots down with vegetable oil or they'd rust right through. I left one out in the rain once when we were camping up near the state park, and it was completely orange by morning. We were sleeping in this old canvas tent that smelled like mildew, and it rained for three days straight.

Sugar rots your teeth out. My dentist told me that when I was twelve, Dr. Henderson. He had these big thick glasses that magnified his eyes so he looked like an owl leaning over you with that drill. I hated that drill. The sound of it just goes right through your skull.

Speaking of the choir robes, my Aunt Linda used to wear one of those big maroon ones. She sang alto down at the First Methodist. Had a voice like an absolute foghorn, God rest her soul. She used to practice her hymns in the kitchen while she was boiling potatoes. She made the best potato salad, always put a little bit of paprika on top so it looked real fancy in the bowl. We'd eat it out on the back porch on the Fourth of July, watching the fireworks go off over the lake. The mosquitoes were just terrible by that lake, though. You had to light those little green coils that smelled like cheap incense just to sit out there for five minutes without getting eaten alive. I don't know what they put in those coils, probably something toxic if you breathe it in too long. 

But anyway... no, my thoughts just don't connect right. I try to stay on one thing, but they just scatter, and people just give me that look, like I skipped half the story, and I can't ever seem to get back on track.

patient.answer:
Yeah, it... it really is causing problems. I mean, I've fallen way behind on my bills. The electric, the water... I just can't keep my days organized anymore. And I've missed a bunch of appointments, too. I even stopped showing up for church and the volunteer stuff I used to do down at the food pantry. I just can't trust ordinary interactions with people, you know? It's like I don't know what they're really thinking or what they're going to do.

Speaking of the food pantry, we used to get these huge pallets of canned green beans. Just boxes and boxes of them. People always donated green beans, but nobody ever brought in corn. I always preferred corn, especially the creamed kind. My grandmother used to make creamed corn from scratch, scraping the cobs with this old silver butter knife she got as a wedding present. It had a little rose pattern on the handle that was mostly worn off. She kept all her good silver in a wooden box lined with blue velvet. It smelled like cedar and old perfume in there. She wouldn't let us touch it unless it was Thanksgiving. We had this big turkey one year that wouldn't even fit in the oven, so my uncle had to take it out to the garage and deep fry it in a turkey fryer. He nearly burned the garage down because he put it in while it was still frozen, and the oil just splattered everywhere. It took weeks to get the grease stains off the concrete floor.

But yeah, I just... I can't keep things straight, and I've stopped going to things because I just can't handle being around people or keeping my schedule organized.

We'd take it out early, before the sun even came up, trying to catch bass. Dave always brought these terrible sandwiches his wife made—bologna and sweet pickles on white bread that would get all soggy in the cooler. The cooler was this bright orange Coleman one, the kind with the white handle that would pinch your fingers if you weren't careful. I pinched my thumb in it once so bad the nail turned black and fell off three weeks later. It was right before I had to help my brother move a piano into his second-floor apartment. Moving a piano with a missing thumbnail is just about the worst thing you can do. The guy at the hardware store told me to soak it in Epsom salts, but I don't think that actually does anything. Epsom salts always just leave a gritty film on the bottom of the tub that you have to scrub out later with a brush. 

But yeah, it's... it's everything I try to talk about. The words just get all tangled up no matter what the subject is.

patient.answer:
No, it hasn't always been like this. It really started changing... I'd say about a year and five months ago. That's when I left the house I shared with my wife and moved into this senior apartment complex. 

My wife, she always kept the house so spotless. We had this big oak dining table that she'd polish every Sunday afternoon. She used that lemon-scented Pledge, you know? The smell of it would just hang in the air all evening. We bought that table at an estate sale out in the county, from this old farmhouse that had a wraparound porch and a rusted-out tractor in the front yard. The guy selling it was wearing these thick suspenders and kept chewing on a toothpick the whole time we were haggling. He had a dog, too, a golden retriever mix that just laid on the porch thumping its tail against the floorboards. I always wanted a dog, but my wife said they track too much mud into the house. She was right, I suppose. Mud is terrible to get out of those Berber carpets. We had beige Berber in the living room, and if you spilled even a drop of coffee on it, it would just soak right in and spread like a bruise. I tried using that foaming carpet cleaner once, the kind in the aerosol can with the little plastic scrub brush on the cap, but it just made the spot look cleaner than the rest of the carpet, which was almost worse. 

But anyway, yeah, the thinking and the talking getting all messed up... that started when I moved into the senior apartment, about a year and five months back.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's disorganized thinking is a new development
doctor.question: Did you used to be able to keep your thoughts organized and on track when talking to people before you moved into the senior apartment?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking to confirm my baseline ability to organize my thoughts and speech before the onset of my disorganized thinking symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yeah, before I moved, I was fine. I could hold a regular conversation. Like I was saying a few minutes ago, about how now I'll start on the rent and end up on the marina and the choir robes and the wires they put in the walls... and how people look at me like I skipped half the story? I never used to do that. It wasn't like that at all. 

Back at the old house, I could just stand out by the chain-link fence and talk to Mr. Henderson for an hour straight, no problem, just keeping right on track. He was our next-door neighbor, the one with the huge vegetable garden. He grew these massive beefsteak tomatoes, big as softballs. He always told me his secret was crushing up dried eggshells and mixing them right into the dirt. We ate a lot of eggs back then so I'd save the shells for him. My wife usually made them scrambled in this heavy cast-iron skillet she got from her mother. You couldn't wash that pan with soap, though. You had to just wipe it out with a paper towel and rub vegetable oil into it while it was still warm. I always thought that was a little unsanitary, just leaving the old grease in there, but she said it seasoned the metal. We kept the oil in this little glass bottle by the stove, but the stopper got glued shut with grease once, and I had to run it under hot water for twenty minutes just to loosen it. The hot water in that house was incredible, though. We had a brand new water heater put in after the basement flooded back in the late nineties, and it would get so hot it could practically take your skin off if you turned the handle too far to the left. 

But yeah, I used to be able to just tell a story from start to finish without losing my place.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's disorganized thinking is a persistent trait or a symptom that varies in intensity
doctor.question: Do you have days where your thoughts seem more connected and easier to explain to others than they do right now?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2

patient.answer:
Not really. I mean... even on the days where maybe I can string a few more sentences together and sound a little clearer, it doesn't matter much. Because for most of the time since I moved into that apartment, I just feel so low. Just useless. I don't even have any interest in the things I used to like doing. 

Like the woodworking. I used to love whittling these little wooden birds out of basswood blocks. Basswood is the best for that because the grain is so tight and it doesn't splinter when you make a fine cut. I had this set of carving knives that came in a leather roll-up pouch. The leather smelled like a saddle shop, you know? Like oil and dust. I bought them from a catalogue that used to come in the mail every month. The mail carrier back then was this guy named Phil who always wore shorts, even in December. He said his legs never got cold, which I always thought was a lie. You can't walk through six inches of snow in shorts and not get cold. Snow gets right into the tops of your boots if you don't wear those gaiter things. I bought a pair of gaiters once for a hunting trip, but they had these plastic snaps that broke the very first time I tried to put them on. Plastic just gets brittle in the cold. It's like those cheap ice scrapers they give away at the gas station—you push too hard on the windshield and the handle snaps right off in your glove. 

But yeah, even if my thoughts are a little less tangled some days, I still just sit there feeling empty and useless, not caring about the carving or anything else.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of hallucinations
doctor.question: Do you ever see things that aren't really there?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about visual hallucinations (seeing things that aren't there), but my symptom profile does not include hallucinations.

patient.answer:
See things? No, I don't... I don't think I've ever seen anything that wasn't there. I mean, my eyesight isn't what it used to be. I had to get bifocals about three years ago because I couldn't read the labels on the soup cans at the grocery store. They make the print so small now, especially on the low-sodium ones. My wife used to buy the low-sodium chicken noodle because she read in a magazine that regular soup has too much salt and it's bad for your blood pressure. The magazine was one of those ones they always have at the dentist's office, with the glossy pages that stick together if somebody spilled coffee on them. Our dentist had this waiting room with these horrible orange vinyl chairs that made a squeaking noise every time you shifted your weight. He had a fish tank in there, too, with these little neon tetras that just swam back and forth all day. I always felt bad for them, stuck in that little glass box with fake plastic plants. Real plants are so much better for aquariums because they help oxygenate the water. I tried to grow a fern once in the living room, but it just turned brown and crispy at the edges. I think it was too close to the heating vent. Those vents would blow hot air right on the curtains and make them billow out like sails on a ship. 

But no, I don't see things that aren't there. Just... just regular things, mostly.
